description:
Wesam Saad introduces perseverance of the saints through the promises of God’s preserving power. He describes the doctrine as God bringing those truly born again through to final salvation, supplying what is needed for them to persevere. The study begins with positive promises before attempting the warning passages raised by listeners. In John 6, he connects the Father’s drawing with Christ raising the person on the last day. John 5 then supplies the present possession of eternal life and the passage from death to life. Saad’s emphasis is confidence in God’s action, rather than a guarantee based on the believer’s independent strength.

Further passages develop that assurance through the Spirit’s pledge, the Shepherd’s protection and God’s faithfulness to sanctify and preserve his people. Saad answers the lost-sheep question by distinguishing the seeking of a person not yet brought to faith from a saved person escaping Christ’s keeping. In 1 Peter, he emphasises both the reserved inheritance and the believer protected by God’s power through faith. The intended response is joy and gratitude, with courage to serve and share the gospel. Questions about willful sin, doubts, backsliding and the warning passages are expressly collected for later discussion. This opening study does not equate perseverance with sinless perfection or complete every objection.

questions.question: What does Saad mean by perseverance of the saints?
questions.answer: He describes God preserving those truly born again so that they continue to the end and are finally glorified. The emphasis is enduring saving faith sustained by God, rather than merely making an outward profession once. Questions about sin and setbacks within that life are reserved for further discussion.

questions.question: How does he connect John 6:44 with final salvation?
questions.answer: Saad connects the person drawn by the Father with the person Christ promises to raise on the last day. He treats the divine drawing as the basis of that assurance, continuing the earlier discussion of spiritual inability and effective calling. The answer follows his reading of the same person throughout the verse.

questions.question: What does he emphasise in the promise of eternal life in John 5?
questions.answer: Saad stresses that the hearer who believes has eternal life, does not come into judgment and has passed from death to life. He reads these together as a present saving possession with an enduring outcome. The argument concerns the believer described in the passage, not an indiscriminate assurance about every profession.

questions.question: What role does the Holy Spirit’s pledge have in the argument?
questions.answer: Saad explains Ephesians 1:13–14 as God sealing the believer with the promised Spirit in view of the inheritance. His deposit illustration emphasises the certainty of God fulfilling his promise. The assurance rests on God’s faithfulness and the pledge he gives rather than a personal achievement that earns the inheritance.

questions.question: How does he use the Good Shepherd’s protection?
questions.answer: Saad follows the promises that Christ’s sheep hear, follow, receive eternal life and will not perish. He emphasises the keeping of both the Son and the Father, rather than an image of the believer supplying the stronger grip. Following Christ belongs within the promise he explains.

questions.question: How does he answer the question about the lost sheep in Luke 15?
questions.answer: Saad reads the parable in the setting of sinners coming to Jesus and religious leaders objecting. He understands the lost sheep as one being sought and brought to faith, rather than a genuinely saved person slipping out of Christ’s keeping. This is the contextual explanation he gives for the objection.

questions.question: What does he draw from 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24?
questions.answer: Saad highlights God as the one who sanctifies and preserves the whole person and who is faithful to bring the calling to completion. He connects the promised preservation with God’s faithfulness rather than the believer’s ability to guarantee the outcome alone. The text is used as a further assurance alongside the Gospel promises.

questions.question: Why distinguish the preserved inheritance from the preserved believer in 1 Peter?
questions.answer: Saad first notes the inheritance’s enduring character, then emphasises that the people themselves are protected by God’s power through faith. His point is not merely that a reward remains somewhere while the believer may never reach it. The passage connects the guarded inheritance with God’s keeping of those born again.

questions.question: What practical response does he seek?
questions.answer: Saad urges joy, gratitude and confidence in God rather than pride in personal ability to remain saved. He also connects assurance with courage in gospel witness, particularly where fear of future failure discourages someone from coming to Christ. He presents the doctrine as a reason to trust God’s keeping.

questions.question: Which questions remain for the following studies?
questions.answer: Saad collects objections from warning passages and questions about doubts, willful sin and backsliding. He does not finish those explanations in this opening session. The promise of preservation must therefore not be recast as a claim that believers never sin or experience a struggle simply because later details are not yet given.
